speaker: bethmyers
text: Welcome to the First District Court of Appeals. We have several cases on our docket this morning, two will be argued. The first that will be argued is N. Ray S. W. Ms. Steer is here on behalf of Appellant. Mr. Thompson is here on behalf of Appalee. Ms. Steer, of your 15 minutes, would you like to reserve any time for rebuttal?

speaker: marystier
text: Yes, please. Could I reserve five minutes?

speaker: bethmyers
text: Yes, and I will keep your time whenever you're ready to begin.

speaker: marystier
text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honor, Counsel, may it please the court. I really doubt that I'm even going to use the full amount of my time. This is a pretty straightforward case. S. W. was taken into custody on suspicion of a robbery that was reported in Avondale. He was Mirandized by Sergeant Roth and questioned about a gun and where he had thrown it. The juvenile magistrate, after a hearing in which Dr. Rothenberg testified that S. W. was not competent to waive his Miranda rights, suppressed those statements made to Sergeant Roth, but also suppressed statements that were later made to Officer Wormuth as Officer Wormuth was taking S. W. to the cruiser. The state's position is that he was not subject to interrogation, so whether he had waived his Miranda rights initially with Sergeant Roth really isn't applicable to what happened with Officer Wormuth. The statement, that statement was voluntary. All he said was, you can let those, can you let those guys go? I did it. It's kind of hard to exactly hear what he said, but that's what he said. And then Officer Wormuth told him not to say anything.

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: Well, yeah, and so I guess there's, you say that he was not subject to interrogation, but he was being interrogated the entire time leading up to that statement. And obviously the officer's reaction she just mentioned suggested that he felt like the child should not say anything. So how do we square that with it's, your position that it's a voluntary statement?

speaker: marystier
text: Well, I think that Officer Wormuth saying, don't say anything, I don't think that that really affects whether or not it's voluntary. What was in the officer's mind? Seth or S. W. was not being interrogated at the time. He had been interrogated by Sergeant Roth as he was walking to the back of the apartment building when they were looking back in the woods to see where the gun was. And then it's clear that there's virtually no words spoken to him by Officer Wormuth. The extent of the conversation between them is S. W. asking what's gonna happen to the stuff that's in his pockets. Officer Wormuth tells him that he, it has to stay with him. And then he asked S. W. if this was a good address for him, this apartment building, to which S. W. said, no, there was no interrogation.

speaker: robertwinkler
text: Ms. Stier, let me ask you, what effect, if any, do you think the on-scene identification of S. W. had?

speaker: marystier
text: I don't think that that has any impact on whether his statement was just a volunteered statement not made during interrogation. He was walked down the street and I think that the victim identified him and Officer Wormuth said into his radio, confirmed, but I'm not even sure that S. W. knew what was happening. He was just being walked down the street to the police cruiser and paused for a second.

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: Well, I guess that's the other point. Like, based on the expert's testimony and the conclusions by the magistrate that you don't challenge on appeal, I mean, he was a very low-functioning child with like, what, a four or five-year-old kind of comprehension level. And when the Miranda rights were read in like 18 seconds, how do we expect someone like that to understand and internalize the significance of the Miranda rights?

speaker: marystier
text: Well, I don't think that that's what we're doing because we are not challenging the suppression of those statements that were made as a result of him being Mirandized. I think if you look at this another way, say, for instance, Sergeant Roth had shown up, I think it was three boys, they were upstairs in this apartment building. If right when he walked up, before he Mirandized S. W., if S. W. said, you can let those guys go, I did it. If he said that, we wouldn't even be talking about this, I don't think, because it would be clear that that's a volunteered statement that wasn't as a result of-

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: Well, but can a child, a 13-year-old, who has the mental functioning capacity of a four or five-year-old, can they voluntarily make a statement like that that is binding on them?

speaker: marystier
text: I don't, I think that then we're getting into his competency to make statements. I don't think there's any question that he made this, that he can make a statement. I think it's whether or not he understands the whole point of Miranda is whether or not a defendant understands that he's voluntarily waiving his rights, not to answer questions when interrogated by police officers.

speaker: bethmyers
text: I had sort of the same question as Judge Bergeron, maybe just a different spin on it. If he's not competent to waive his rights, if he can't do that, how can he voluntarily give any statement? I know nobody's argued that, but it does seem a little contradictory.

speaker: marystier
text: I think maybe that would go to, maybe the weight that you gave the statement that he made, I think it would go to that, but I don't think that it would be a matter of suppressing it because of him not, because of him waiving his Miranda rights, because this was the, I don't think, I think you have to set aside the fact that Miranda doesn't apply in this case because it's a voluntary statement not made as a result of an interrogation. I think whether his statement itself, what the weight that you give that, I think maybe that's something you argue at trial, whether a 13-year-old boy can say, I did it. I think you would argue that maybe, he didn't know what he was talking about, but I don't think that that's subject to suppression because of him.

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: Well, I guess like how much do we take into the, to account the background context? I mean, he was apprehended at gunpoint. He's been arrested. There've been a number of like, you're gonna be in trouble if you don't tell me these things type of questions. There's people screaming in the background. There's all these police cruisers. Like, do we take that into account in assessing the voluntariness of the statement?

speaker: marystier
text: I think that when you're looking at it in terms of whether or not Miranda was violated, I think it's starts and stops with whether or not he was being interrogated. And his statement was a purely volunteered statement. I think the fact that he's a 13-year-old boy with maybe below average intelligence, that's probably a question for trial whether or not his statement should be credited. And that all feeds into it. You know, the people screaming, he's obviously scared. You know, Sergeant Roth was asking him repeatedly where the gun was and where he had thrown it. Obviously that was a lot of pressure, but I don't think that that makes his statement subject to suppression for a violation of Miranda.

speaker: bethmyers
text: Can I ask you one other follow-up question? In a lot of the cases, what happens is somebody is given their Miranda warnings. They choose to exercise those rights. Then there's a break in time and they're in custody but not being interrogated and they volunteer a statement. All those cases are premised on the person initially understanding that they had the right to remain silent and exercise that right for a period of time. That's what's kind of making this case a little different for me because he didn't have that ability when it stopped. You know, there is a clear demarcation of a few minutes where there was no questioning. But how do you handle those cases that I just alluded to?

speaker: marystier
text: Well, I think in those cases, it again comes down to whether or not it's just a spontaneous statement or whether it came as a result of an interrogation. For instance, I think there are cases where someone's been Mirandized and then they're put back into a holding cell. If they blurt something out to whoever, the corrections officer who's walking them to the cell, I don't think that that's subject to suppression for under Miranda. However, if the correction officer, as he's walking him, says, why don't you come clean? I think then that that could still be considered interrogation that the defendant is referring, that the defendant is responding to. And then I think you have to look and see whether or not he voluntarily waived his Miranda rights.

speaker: bethmyers
text: And you have about one more minute if you'd like to reserve five.

speaker: marystier
text: I'll reserve the rest of my time unless the court has any more questions.

speaker: bethmyers
text: Any questions? No. Mr. Thompson, you have 15 minutes.

speaker: joshuathompson
text: Good morning. May it please the court, counsel. I cannot emphasize enough what the Ohio Supreme Court said in State v. Barker, 2016, Ohio 2708, paragraph 26, that absent the state's compliance with Miranda and a suspect's valid waiver of his Fifth Amendment rights, even voluntary statements are inadmissible. This ultimately makes a lot of sense because the alternative, that someone who does not understand their rights can still make a voluntary statement, makes no sense.

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: So just to make sure I understand your position and kind of following up on Judge Meyer's question, are you taking, is it your position that if there is an ineffective Miranda for whatever reason, whether that's lack of comprehension or they didn't read them the rights, that no subsequent statement, no matter how far removed from that Miranda warning can be considered voluntary? Or is there a timeline some point in the future where it could become voluntary?

speaker: joshuathompson
text: There is no timeline, but intervening events, I believe such as perhaps interacting with a lawyer on their behalf or regaining competency and then making a statement, those would change the math, I believe.

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: What about like consultation with a parent for a juvenile, would that break the chain?

speaker: joshuathompson
text: It's a factor in the totality of circumstances, but I don't believe it would be a hard line that absolutely broke the chain. No, we really, we don't have any challenge here. No question that SW could not validly waive his Fifth Amendment rights.

speaker: bethmyers
text: And let me interrupt you there. And that's because he didn't have the capability to understand them, correct?

speaker: joshuathompson
text: Correct.

speaker: bethmyers
text: So going back to the questions that I think we were all asking Ms. Stier, doesn't that impact the voluntariness of his statement to begin with? And nobody is arguing that really, are they? Nobody argued that his statement was involuntary because of his competency.

speaker: joshuathompson
text: Well, I think if you cannot understand your Miranda rights, your statement is, or your admission is inherently involuntary.

speaker: bethmyers
text: So here, then let me give a hypothetical. Let's say that it came upon him before anybody asked him any questions, as Ms. Stier in her hypothetical said, he volunteered, I did it. Is it your position that because ultimately he wouldn't have been competent to waive his Miranda rights, that he's not competent to make that statement and that statement's inadmissible?

speaker: joshuathompson
text: The police went to him first?

speaker: bethmyers
text: Well, they're on the scene investigating. Yes, they approach him. And as they approach him, he's not, well, I guess he's not in custody. Let's say he's in custody and they haven't asked him any question yet. He's handcuffed, he can't leave. They've even maybe arrested him. They haven't read him his rights, but he volunteers a statement.

speaker: joshuathompson
text: Because he's a juvenile, I still say yes, that it should be suppressed. And that's because children are due a special care. In Galt, they said the greatest care must be taken to ensure that the admission was voluntary in the sense not only that it was not coerced or suggested, but that it was not the product of ignorance of right or an adolescent fantasy, fright, or despair. And I think that's ultimately what we have here. We know SW is only 13. He's arrested at gunpoint with two of his friends. He's got a low level of intelligence, limited prior police contact, no parent or guardian or lawyer available to him at the time. Sergeant Roth was aggressive with him, cursed at him, consistently pressured him to tell the officers the gun's location, told him he'd be in more trouble if he didn't tell him where the gun was. Also told him that if he was truthful, things would go better for him. Then ultimately SW goes through an identification procedure where he hears he was positively ID'd. And all of that occurs before the admission. But even then the interrogation didn't really stop. Officer Wormuth asked if SW lived at the apartment where he was arrested. He was doing a search when the admission was made and being placed in a police cruiser. And ultimately I believe the admission was made in the interest of protecting his friends. So I think that fits right into being a product of ignorance of his, not just ignorance of his rights, but adolescent fantasy, fear, or despair. So even if we reach this totality of the circumstances, question, because I don't think we need to get there under Barker and Dickerson, but if we do, then SW in particular was not a person who could make a voluntary statement.

speaker: bethmyers
text: And is that under any circumstances, no matter when in this timeline he confessed, would your position be no, he couldn't make a voluntary statement?

speaker: joshuathompson
text: If he walked into a police station and said, I need to tell everyone that I just robbed someone, I don't think that would be suppressed. I think that would be voluntary. But here where there's police-

speaker: bethmyers
text: And where are you drawing the line? I mean, is it-

speaker: joshuathompson
text: The police interaction, sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt.

speaker: bethmyers
text: So it's not a temporal, it's not just a time thing.

speaker: joshuathompson
text: No, I believe it's a police interaction situation here that because the police are seeking information from him, that's when we have to get into this totality of circumstances. And in this particular scenario, like the judge found, this was a continuing process. I think Miranda does apply. It's questionable whether the Miranda rights were valid given they were given so quickly and in such a sort of desperate set of circumstances. But even if they were, clearly SW didn't understand those rights and didn't voluntarily waive them because he was incapable. And the circumstances were such that anything that he did was out of fright or despair.

speaker: robertwinkler
text: Mr. Thompson, let me ask this question. We're all aware of the deficits under which SW was laboring, but from the point that he was handed off to Officer Weermuth in a limited conversation that concerned his property, whether he lived in that building, and then a statement. Can we take anything from that conversation? And I guess my point is he seemed to respond appropriately. He was concerned about the property in his pockets. The officer said, is that your building? He said, no. Can we consider that?

speaker: joshuathompson
text: Well, ultimately I don't think the state is challenging his competency, but I do think it could be considered for the fact that it is a continuing interrogation. Questions are still being asked.

speaker: robertwinkler
text: You mean a question like, is that your building? Is that interrogation?

speaker: joshuathompson
text: For a 13-year-old incompetent boy, I think any question is a question where the police are seeking information. It's a custodial interrogation, a custodial question. If there are no further questions, I ask that the court affirm the granting of the motion to suppress.

speaker: bethmyers
text: Any further questions from the panel? No. Thank you, Mr. Thompson. Ms. Steer, you have six minutes.

speaker: marystier
text: Thank you, Your Honor. Judge Winkler, if I can go back to the question you were asking whether or not the questions regarding if this is where you live and answering his question about what's gonna happen to the stuff in his pocket. Those aren't interrogate, those are questions, they're questions seeking information, but they're not interrogation about a crime. There's plenty of times when police officers ask a defendant their name and other identifying information that's not an interrogation. Miranda, in Miranda, the court said that it applies to, there's two elements, custody and interrogation. In this case, there's no question that SW was in custody. He was in custody when Sergeant Roth was talking to him and he was in custody when Wormuth was walking him to the cruiser, but there simply is no interrogation happening. There was no questioning whether or not his statement should be credited or given any weight, that's a question for trial. It's not a question, it's not something that's subject to suppression under Miranda. And I don't think that just because he's a juvenile and I understand his young age and I understand that he was low intelligence, but I don't think that there's a separate rule for juveniles as far as volunteered statements, spontaneous statements outside of Miranda. And the state submits that Miranda doesn't apply in this case. So the state would ask that the judgment be reversed as to the statements made to Officer Wormuth.

speaker: bethmyers
text: Thank you. Any other questions for Ms. Steer? No. Thank you both for your arguments this morning. We will take the case under submission, and give you a timely written opinion.

speaker: marystier
text: Thank you.

speaker: bethmyers
text: You will bring the next parties into the courtroom, please. Good morning. The next case on our docket this morning, State versus Moss. Ms. Callaway is here on behalf of Appellant. Ms. Barnett is here on behalf of Apogee. Ms. Callaway, you have 15 minutes to argue this morning. Would you like to reserve any time?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: Good morning. Thank you, Your Honor. I'd like to reserve three minutes for rebuttal, please. All right. And whenever you're ready, I will keep your time. Okay, thank you. May it please the court. This case is pretty straightforward. And I know the court comes prepared having reviewed the briefs and understands the facts. And so I'm not going to rehash it unless there's questions about it. This is a pretty straightforward sentencing issue. In this case, the defendant was sentenced for, he was arrested for a bunch of charges. I think 11. He was sentenced for the felony to 18 months in prison. And after that sentencing took place, he went back and was sentenced on the misdemeanor charges and the court imposed additional time that was consecutive to the felonies. And so the issue before the court, I'm not sure exactly what the municipal court judge was thinking here. There isn't a lot on the record about it. I know that prior to the Supreme Court's case in Polis, which is described in detail in my brief, there was some confusion under 29-29-41 exactly what was being communicated with that statute. There were some provisions that some of the districts in Ohio thought were in conflict with each other, but the Polis court clarified exactly what is meant by that statute. And the upshot of it in Polis is that sentences for misdemeanors have to be run concurrent with time for felonies. And so I think this case is really important.

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: Does that hinge though on the defendant actually being in the midst of serving time for the felony?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: No. I understand what the court is getting at, but the idea of someone serving concurrent time is a legal fiction, right? You can't actually do two things at the same time. And so when the sentences are imposed at the same time, the court must order them to be served concurrently. I understand this is a little bit of a factual discrepancy because the time was already served on the felony and then the misdemeanor charge came in for sentencing after that. But because the idea of concurrent sentences is a legal fiction and because the statute doesn't say, well, if they're sentenced separately, that means that you can serve them consecutively. There's no exception there. We have to follow the plain language of the statute, which says that the sentences must be ordered to be served concurrently. And so it doesn't appear based on the language of the statute or the court's decision interpretation in Polis that there's an exception there for if they're sentenced separately. This case is important because of this function that we have in Hamilton County where cases can be put on the suspended docket. I think in most jurisdictions, the suspended docket doesn't exist and it creates an opportunity for what happened here, which is very nefarious for the defendant because the defendants often aren't even aware that cases are being put on the suspended docket. When the cases come through room A, the cases get split off immediately and the defendants sometimes usually aren't even aware of it. And that's what happened in this case. The defendant was concentrated on the felony, the cases were going on, the felony was being set and plea or your trial settings and the misdemeanors were just hanging out there. There was never any court date.

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: And the purpose of that rule, at least as I read it, is that it is basically to give the defendant the benefit of the statute and to avoid having the courts have to deal with the misdemeanor while the felony proceedings are ongoing. Is that fair?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: I agree. I'm not criticizing the rule per se. And I agree that that was the reason for the suspended docket and it makes sense for judicial efficiency. But what happens is that I've seen this happen, I know this isn't in the record, but just anecdotally, these cases, the misdemeanors fall in the cracks. And usually-

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: Yeah, what are the safeguards here to prevent this exact scenario?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: I don't know the answer to that. To be honest with you, as a practitioner, this was always a huge fear of mine that I would forget about the misdemeanors that were on the suspended docket. I think that that's what happened in this case. The retained counsel never got word that there were misdemeanor charges here, never entered a notice of appearance, took over the felonies. The appointed counsel just figured that felony, retained counsel was taking care of everything, and then nothing was ever done. And so I would suggest that the safeguard then is 292941, which says that the misdemeanors must be run concurrently. And so the stopgap measure for having somebody serve multiple sentences like this is the plain language of the statute, which says that misdemeanor time must be run concurrent with felony sentences. And so I-

speaker: robertwinkler
text: Ms. Callaway, let me ask you this, doesn't it say served concurrently? And if he's already served his sentence for the felonies, isn't the judge free to sentence on the misdemeanors?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: Well, I understand. Sorry, I understand the court's question, but again, I would just point the court back to the idea of what a concurrent sentence is. A concurrent sentence is a legal fiction, and the idea that you can serve two sentences at the same time is something that we've all just decided is possible, even though I'm not sure in the laws of physics that that's an actual thing, but the courts and the legislature have all decided like, okay, we're gonna operate within this legal fiction because that's our preference that the sentences all be served at the same time. And so I don't think that these cases that got siphoned off, either I'm gonna say by accident, I'm not gonna, it wasn't on purpose, the state didn't do this, this was an accident, that that somehow now gives this defendant, it can be penalized twice when the statute requires plainly that the sentences be ordered to be served concurrently. And so that language served concurrently, again, is a legal fiction, and there's nothing that stops the court from operating or operationalizing the legal fiction that it be served concurrently, whether the sentence are sentenced to be served on the same day, or whether the sentences happen a month apart or two years apart, the legal fiction is still there.

speaker: bethmyers
text: And so- And so I understand your argument. In this case, if he had been sentenced to in felony court and then taken immediately down to municipal court for sentencing, those would have been served concurrently. And the fact that it didn't happen immediately should make no legal difference.

speaker: wendycalaway
text: Correct. The court's decision in Polis, I think is unambiguous about that. This case is a little bit factually different from Polis just because of the amount of time, but that is correct. That's my position. Whether it was an hour or two years, the statute says that the municipal court had to sentence, had to impose a concurrent sentence.

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: But is that, does that argument only make sense if the claims are related? Like, in other words, in your two-year scenario, if he picked up a misdemeanor two years later after being sentenced and serving time on a felony and there's no relation, like you wouldn't be taking this position in that circumstance, would you?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: Well, that's not what happened in this case. These cases all arose out of the same traffic, the same incident. So these were all part of the same course of conduct. But no, even if these had been separate, I believe under Polis, that was the factual scenario in Polis. And the other case I cited from Belmont County in my brief, that happened. I think it was a probation violation got revoked and the court imposed a sentence and then they picked up a separate charge separate from that probation violation and the court imposed separate sentences. And on appeal, the appellate court said, no, under 292941, sentences must be served concurrently even when they arise from separate factual incidents. So this was a probation violation and a new charge. And so that wouldn't be my position. I believe that the sentences must be served concurrently. Now, in that case, they're obviously being served at the same time. If he picked up a probation violation, served his time, then came back and picked up a new charge. No, I don't think those sentences have to be served concurrently because they do arise from separate instances.

speaker: bethmyers
text: And so- Procedurally in this case, the municipal judge would order a sentence and then find that there's credit for all the time served. Is that procedurally what you would suggest should happen?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: My suggestion would be that if the court feels that it needs to order additional time, that it order on the sentencing entry that it be served concurrently with the felony time.

speaker: bethmyers
text: But that, I think, gets to Judge Winkler's question. It's over. So concurrent what? Wouldn't then it have to be credit for time served? I don't think so. Let's say the judge did say concurrent and that gets to concurrent what?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: Yeah, it gets concurrent to the felony sentence that was a companion case here. And so I don't think that that's any different than what they would have done if they had sentenced on the same day. Courts in their entries all the time, right? Concurrent to case number X or concurrent to case number Y. That's all the court had to do here. 60 days concurrent to, and then the case number of the felony that was a companion to this case.

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: But I think the question that both my colleagues are getting to is that is it possible to serve concurrently a sentence that has already been completely served? Like if you get it in this scenario, if the judge has said serve this 60 days concurrent to this felony charge, is that possible given that the felony sentence had already been served?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: I understand the question. My answer to the question is yes. It's possible in the same way it's possible to serve any kind of concurrent sentence. A person is ordered to serve 12 months for a breaking and entering and 12 months for a drug possession. And those sentences are ordered to be served concurrently. They're serving them at the same time. That's a legal fiction. This in the exact same way, the municipal court in this case should have ordered the 60 days to be served concurrent to the felony time serving at the same time, just the same way they would have if they had ordered the sentence to be served on the same day. I understand the court's troubled over this, whether they can be served at the same time once it's already been served. But with all due respect, I feel that the court is fighting the idea of the concurrent sentence. I mean, no one can actually serve a concurrent sentence. This is a policy decision that the legislature has put forth to say, we want these sentences to be imposed concurrently. And so there is no difference in saying that this should be served concurrent to the case number. So that's my answer to that.

speaker: robertwinkler
text: Ms. Callaway, I'm in substantial agreement with what you're saying here, but in the Polis case, didn't the sentencing judge have Mr. or Mrs. Polis in front of him at the same time that he or she sentenced the defendant concurrently?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: I believe that's correct, yes.

speaker: robertwinkler
text: And this is sort of an anomaly. Couldn't Judge Bender have sentenced your client to 18 months in the Department of Corrections and merely credited the time, I'm sorry, in the Justice Center and credited the time that he had already served? I mean, that was within her authority, wasn't it?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: I think the time, I'm sorry, I think the time has to be served concurrently under the statute.

speaker: robertwinkler
text: But if she credited it, if she credited the time, wouldn't the effect is it was served concurrently?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: Yes, I mean, we wouldn't-

speaker: robertwinkler
text: You wouldn't be serving it?

speaker: wendycalaway
text: I'm sorry, Your Honor.

speaker: robertwinkler
text: That's okay, go ahead.

speaker: wendycalaway
text: Yes, we wouldn't be here. I certainly wouldn't appeal that. And so the effect would be the same. And so as long as the client isn't harmed by it, that's fine with me. I think the more proper way to do it in the entry is to say that it's being served concurrently. But if you wanna effectuate the same outcome and not use that language and make it more logically consistent, then yes, that would be a way to do it as well.

speaker: robertwinkler
text: Well, but my point is that a sentencing judge in the initial court could have sentenced to 18 months and your client served about 11, I believe. So wouldn't he have served a balance of that sentence over in the Justice Center? Do you understand my question?

speaker: joshuathompson
text: You're saying that-

speaker: robertwinkler
text: He served a state sentence and then there was a balance left and they would transfer it back to the Justice Center to serve out the balance of his misdemeanor sentence and they would have been served concurrently.

speaker: wendycalaway
text: That is correct.

speaker: bethmyers
text: Yep. And you are out of time, Ms. Callaway. I'll let you finish that answer to that question. And then if the panel has any other questions.

speaker: wendycalaway
text: Yes, I appreciate the judge's question and I agree that that could have been a possible outcome in this case, but that's not what happened. And so because of the way that the court imposed the sentence, it had to be served concurrently under the statute. Thank you.

speaker: bethmyers
text: Thank you. Any other questions from the panel? Ms. Barnett, you have 15 minutes.

speaker: rebeccabarnett
text: Thank you. Good morning, your honors. May it please the court opposing counsel. I would start by saying that I disagree that this case is straightforward as all the issues that have been discussed so far including the suspended docket. I think this case is actually rather unique for a few reasons. First and foremost, it was brought about by the use of the suspended docket, which is unique to Hampton County. So we don't have case law from other jurisdictions about how to handle this.

speaker: pierrebergeron
text: And would you agree with my characterization that the suspended docket, at least it's embodied in the rule, is designed to preserve this type of essentially benefit for the defendants and preserve judicial economy. Is that fair or would you characterize it differently?

speaker: rebeccabarnett
text: Yes, absolutely. I would agree with that characterization. Practicing in municipal court, oftentimes we get cases where there are some misdemeanors and we get wind that there are felonies. So then it becomes a discussion, why don't we put this one suspended docket, especially if they're arising out of the same incident, let's see how that plays out.
